cards.h: How politics was studied before the 1950s
cards.b:
An approach is a way of looking. It decides what questions you ask and what evidence you use.

Before the Second World War, political science mostly used traditional approaches. These were value-based, used history and law, and focused on the state and its institutions.

This is the oldest approach. It starts with values and reasoning, not data. It asks: what is the ideal state, and what is justice?

  • Thinkers: Plato, Aristotle, Hegel, T.H. Green.
  • Strength: it gives us goals and ideals to aim for.
  • Weakness: it can be abstract and hard to test. Critics say it is speculative.

This approach says you can only understand political ideas in their historical setting. Ideas come from real problems of their age.

  • Thinkers: Machiavelli used history as a tool; Sabine and Dunning wrote histories of political thought.
  • Strength: it gives context. Hobbes makes more sense when you know about the English Civil War.
  • Weakness: history can be read selectively, and the past does not always predict the present.

This approach studies formal structures: constitutions, legislatures, executives and courts.

  • Thinkers: James Bryce (Modern Democracies), Herman Finer, Harold Laski.
  • Strength: it is concrete and descriptive. It is good for comparing governments.
  • Weakness: it ignores informal politics like caste, pressure groups and personality. A constitution on paper can differ a lot from politics in practice.

This approach sees the state mainly as a legal body that makes and enforces law. Politics is studied through laws, rights and courts.

  • Thinkers: Jean Bodin and Hobbes (sovereignty as the source of law), A.V. Dicey (rule of law), John Austin (law as the command of the sovereign).
  • Weakness: it is very narrow. Law is only one part of political life.

• They are value-laden: they openly judge what is good.
  • They are state-centric: the state is the main unit of study.
  • They are descriptive and prescriptive, rather than explanatory or predictive.
  • They rely on reasoning, history and legal texts, not surveys or statistics.

After 1945, American scholars felt traditional approaches could not explain real political behaviour. They could not explain why democracy collapsed in Weimar Germany or why people voted for fascists.

The criticism was that traditional approaches were too formal, too normative and too narrow. This opened the door for the behavioural revolution, which is the next lesson.

The institutional and legal approaches still matter a lot in India. Debates on the basic structure doctrine (Kesavananda Bharati, 1973), the anti-defection law, or Governor's powers are mainly legal-institutional.

But you can only explain coalition politics or caste voting with newer approaches. A strong answer shows both.

"Critically examine the traditional approaches to the study of politics."

Structure: define approach, describe the four types with one thinker each, give common features, then the behavioural critique. End by saying modern theory has a revival of new institutionalism (March and Olsen, 1984), which shows that institutions still matter.

quiz.q: Which approach focuses on constitutions and formal structures?
quiz.w: The institutional approach studies formal structures of government.
Austin's analytical jurisprudence defined law as the command of the sovereign.

quiz.q: A key weakness of the institutional approach is that it…
quiz.w: It ignores informal forces like caste, pressure groups and personalities.
James March and Johan Olsen (1984) brought institutions back in.
